approach.expect: From the Beverly Creek Trailhead (end of FR-9737-112, at ~3,600 ft), start on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391. After a short, mellow half mile paralleling Beverly Creek, bear right at the signed junction onto the Bean Creek Trail (#1391A), leaving the Turnpike Trail behind. The Bean Creek Trail climbs steadily through forest and then opens into Bean Creek Basin around the 2.5-mile mark — a broad, flower-choked meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats; this is the scenic highlight of the approach and a natural rest/water stop. Bean Creek itself is the last dependable water source. Its crossings are easy rock-hops by mid-to-late summer but can be swift, cold, and genuinely hazardous during May–June snowmelt, so plan accordingly if going early season. Beyond the basin the trail (tread becomes intermittent in the upper meadows) climbs switchbacks up to Earl Pass at roughly 6,200 ft — the broad saddle on the divide between the Bean Creek and Standup Creek drainages, about 3.5–4 miles and ~2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead. This pass has scattered flat tent sites and is the standard high camp for parties splitting the trip, or the pack-cache point for day-scramblers. From Earl Pass, leave the trail and pick up the boot path climbing the southwest ridge directly toward the summit. This final ~800 vertical feet is the crux of the trip: a sustained, unrelenting class 2 scramble on loose scree, sand, and broken rock with only an intermittent climbers' track — go slow, test holds, and be mindful of kicking rock onto anyone below. The ridge tops out on Earl Peak's 7,036-ft summit with a full panorama of the Stuart Range from Mt. Stuart to Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail.

approach.expect: Start at the Stafford Creek Trailhead (Trail #1359), Cle Elum Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, at the end of Stafford Creek Road (FR 9703), which leaves North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) past 29 Pines Campground — a small, often-overflowing lot for roughly 20 cars (Northwest Forest Pass required). From the trailhead, Stafford Creek Trail #1359 climbs at a gentle-to-moderate grade through dry ponderosa/lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek for the first mile (a short rerouted, steeper switchback section around 0.5 mile bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread). The trail continues gaining gradually along the creek — figure roughly 3,000 ft of gain spread over the approach — reaching a signed junction with the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) at about 3.5–3.8 miles; this crossing of Stafford Creek is the last reliable, easy water source before the high country and is worth topping off here. Bear right (east/north) at the junction to stay on the Navaho Pass approach. Around 4.5 miles the trail opens into a large, marshy subalpine meadow with established campsites and a feeder stream — the usual base camp for parties splitting the trip over two days, and another water source. Beyond camp the trail crosses the barren, eroded 'Moon Landing' stretch (sparse vegetation, serpentine/greenstone talus) before a final push to Navaho Pass (~6,000 ft) around mile 5.5. A commonly used shortcut leaves the main trail where two creek forks merge around the 3-mile mark, climbing steep, loose slopes directly up the northeast-facing drainage to the col below Navaho's southeast ridge — it saves close to 2 miles of trail hiking but is steeper, unmaintained, and involves loose scree/dirt, so most parties use it only for one direction of the trip. Total car-to-summit is on the order of 11–13 miles round trip with about 4,000–4,200 ft of gain depending on which junction/shortcut combination is used. Note: this trail corridor has had closures tied to the Labor Mountain Fire and storm damage; Forest Service order 06-17-03-2026-14 closed Stafford Creek Trail #1359 from May 20 through December 31, 2026 unless rescinded sooner, but that order is no longer posted on the Okanogan-Wenatchee alerts page (checked September 26, 2026) — verify current trail status with the Cle Elum Ranger District (509-852-1100) before heading in. A second off-trail variant leaves the trail right after the Stafford Creek crossing and climbs directly into the open bowl between Earl Peak and Navaho Peak to about 5,000 ft, scrambles north to the ridgeline near 6,000 ft, then follows the west/southwest ridge to the summit — a different line than the northeast-drainage shortcut.

expect.name: Stafford Creek Trail #1359 to Navaho Pass
expect.notes: From the small road-end lot, Trail #1359 leaves at an easy grade through dry ponderosa and lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek; a short rerouted section of steeper switchbacks near the half-mile mark bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread. The creek crossing in the meadows is the last easy water and worth topping off at. Stay on #1359 at the signed Standup Creek Trail junction, and the trail opens into a large marshy subalpine meadow with a feeder stream and established campsites — the usual overnight base. Above the meadow the tread leaves the trees and switchbacks up open, rocky, sparsely vegetated slope for the last stretch to the pass.
expect.season: July into October. Snow patches linger on the upper ridge into July, when poles and light traction are worthwhile.
hazards: No water and essentially no shade above the meadows, on ground that bakes on a warm afternoon
Loose scree over dirt on the climbers' path onto the ridge, steepening quickly and easy to push down onto a party below
Slopes on either flank of the summit ridge are looser and steeper than they look from above
The trail corridor has been closed for fire and storm damage — check current status before driving in
expect.baseFinding: THE SUMMIT PATH IS NOW MORE WORN THAN THE TRAIL IT LEAVES, AND THE WRONG TURN HAS A NAME. Navaho Pass is unmistakable ground — small, rocky, sparsely vegetated and wind-exposed, with the Stuart Range filling the view — and it is where the trail meets the old crest trail along the county line. Head EAST out of the pass, paralleling the range. The old boot-path junction that descriptions still mention has effectively vanished: the beaten track now IS the summit path, more worn than the crest trail beside it, so the thing to look for is the most-used tread rather than a faint branch. If instead you follow the connecting ridge LEFT from the pass, you are heading for Wrong Turn Peak, which is what it is called and why. Two more confusions worth knowing: the prominent peak straight ahead on the walk in is Little Navaho, not this one, and the final ridge throws up several false tops before the true summit, which is small — barely higher than a rocky outcrop just east of it. On the way down, do not follow the southeast ridge all the way toward Little Navaho; there are cliffs below it.

expect.name: Stafford Creek meadow camps below Navaho Pass
expect.notes: This is the camp for Navaho Peak's south slopes and effectively the only one worth using on that side. From the Stafford Creek trailhead the trail climbs gently for the first mile beside the creek, then steepens as it pulls away from it, crosses a marshy open meadow, and reaches these camps at around five miles. Navaho Pass is another half mile up a bare serpentine slope at about 6,000 feet, and the south slopes above the pass are walking and easy scrambling to the summit. Most parties do the whole thing car to car and the camp is the contingency: a late start, a hot afternoon, or a group that wants the summit at dawn. It is also the hinge of the standard two-day loop that links Navaho Pass with the Bean Creek side and comes out at a different trailhead. The meadow is buggy in early summer and the burn scar in the drainage has changed shade and blowdown patterns, so expect the walking to be rougher than an older description suggests.
expect.water: The reason this camp exists. Stafford Creek and a side stream come down the rock faces at the meadow edge and run into late summer in most years, and this is the last dependable water before the pass. Above the meadow there is nothing: the final half mile of bare serpentine to Navaho Pass and the whole of the south slopes above it are completely dry, and on a hot east-side day that is four or five hours of climbing on what you carry.
expect.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery, and no connection to the Enchantment system. Northwest Forest Pass at the Stafford Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet here and the drainage is normally under a full burn ban by July. The Stafford Creek road and trail were inside the 2025 fire closure and were still subject to repair-work closures afterwards, so this is the site most likely to be legally unreachable on any given date — check before you drive.
expect.capacity: Established sites in the timber along the edge of a large meadow, with room for several parties; this is a popular long-weekend base camp and can hold a half dozen tents on a summer Saturday

value.water: The reason this camp exists. Stafford Creek and a side stream come down the rock faces at the meadow edge and run into late summer in most years, and this is the last dependable water before the pass. Above the meadow there is nothing: the final half mile of bare serpentine to Navaho Pass and the whole of the south slopes above it are completely dry, and on a hot east-side day that is four or five hours of climbing on what you carry.
value.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery, and no connection to the Enchantment system. Northwest Forest Pass at the Stafford Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet here and the drainage is normally under a full burn ban by July. The Stafford Creek trail was closed through much of 2026 after the 2025 fire and has reopened, as the Cle Elum Ranger District's trail crew reported on September 25, 2026; many campsites along it burned, so pick a site clear of dead and burned trees.
value.capacity: Established sites in the timber along the edge of a large meadow, with room for several parties; this is a popular long-weekend base camp and can hold a half dozen tents on a summer Saturday

expect.cal: The Stafford Creek trailhead access/trail was reported closed due to Labor Mountain Fire damage as of the last check - confirm current road/trail status before planning a trip.

days.note: From the Stafford Creek trailhead, follow Stafford Creek through meadows to Navaho Pass (~5.5 mi, ~3,000 ft gain), then turn onto the southwest ridge / south slopes for a Class 2 scramble to the summit. Descend by reversing the same route.
days.title: Car-to-car via Stafford Creek and Navaho Pass

schedule.label: Leave Stafford Creek trailhead
schedule.detail: Start early to beat the heat on the exposed upper slopes and finish at a reasonable hour.

schedule.label: Reach Navaho Pass
schedule.detail: ~5.5 miles and ~3,000 ft gained through Stafford Creek Meadows; junction with the old County Line Trail.

schedule.label: Begin southwest ridge / south slopes scramble
schedule.detail: Steep, loose Class 2 terrain for the final ~700-1,000 ft to the summit; snow patches possible into early summer.

schedule.label: Summit Navaho Peak (7,223 ft)
schedule.detail: Small summit with room for only a few people; views of the Enchantments, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and Rainier.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the ascent route back through Navaho Pass and down Stafford Creek.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Total elapsed time typically 8.5-9 hours car-to-car.

days.objective: Summit Navaho Peak and return to the trailhead

expect.totalNote: A single long day hike/scramble: about 13 miles round trip with roughly 4,200 ft of gain, typically 8.5-9 hours car-to-car via Stafford Creek Trail to Navaho Pass then the southwest ridge/south slopes - not an overnight trip for the standard approach.

expect: Lingering snowfields on the upper bowl/ridge into July — can obscure the route and create fall/glissade hazard on steep sections
Afternoon thunderstorms with lightning exposure on the open ridge and summit
Loose talus and blocky terrain above ~6,000 ft — rockfall risk onto parties below
Active Forest Service closure (hazard trees, fire-damaged terrain) on Trail #1359 through Dec 31, 2026
Long, mostly waterless upper approach — carry sufficient water
